name: Matcha / Green Tea
summary: The 40,000-person Ohsaki cohort linked 5+ cups daily to 26% lower cardiovascular mortality, and a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found green tea catechins significantly lowered LDL and total cholesterol; L-theanine boosts alpha waves for calm focus.
how: Ceremonial matcha 1-2g (1 tsp) whisked into 60-80mL of 80C water, 1-3 times daily; or 3-5 cups of quality sencha or gyokuro.
safety: Caffeine ~70mg per matcha serving - limit if sensitive or pregnant (200mg/day cap). Reduces iron absorption; drink between meals. EGCG supplements above 800mg/day are linked to rare liver toxicity - whole tea is safer. May interact with warfarin, beta-blockers and some chemotherapy agents.
origin: Central to the tea ceremony for 800 years; Zen monks drank matcha to stay alert in meditation.

name: Wasabi
summary: A 12-week RCT in 72 older Japanese adults found daily wasabi (0.8mg 6-MITC) significantly improved working and episodic memory; isothiocyanates also show antibacterial activity against H. pylori, E. coli and S. aureus in vitro.
how: Grate fresh wasabi root on a sharkskin grater and use within 15 minutes, 1-2 tsp with meals. Most commercial 'wasabi' is dyed horseradish - seek genuine Wasabia japonica or supplements standardized to 6-MITC.
safety: Potent mucous-membrane irritant; use small amounts. May aggravate gastritis or GERD. No significant interactions at culinary doses, but high supplemental doses have anti-platelet effects - caution with anticoagulants.
origin: Eaten with raw fish for centuries as flavor and antimicrobial protection against food poisoning.

name: Shiso
summary: A clinical trial found perilla seed extract significantly improved seasonal allergic rhinoconjunctivitis versus placebo; rosmarinic acid suppresses IgE-mediated histamine release, and perilla seed oil is 54-64% omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid.
how: 5-10 fresh leaves daily in salads, sushi or as wraps; perilla seed oil 1-2 tsp daily as dressing; dried shiso tea 3-5g steeped, 2-3 times daily; or standardized leaf extract per label.
safety: Very safe at culinary doses. Perilla ketone (in wild, not culinary, varieties) is a lung toxin in livestock; human risk from food shiso is negligible. Mild sedative effect - caution with CNS depressants. Perilla oil may add to anticoagulant effects.
origin: A Kampo and culinary staple for over 1,000 years, prescribed for colds, nausea and seafood allergy.

name: Kudzu / Kuzu
summary: Harvard/McLean laboratory studies found kudzu extract significantly reduced binge drinking in heavy drinkers, cutting beers consumed and slowing sip rate; puerarin also improved coronary blood flow in clinical studies, and Kakkon-to shows antiviral activity against influenza.
how: Extract standardized to puerarin, 500-1500mg/day for alcohol reduction. Kuzu starch 1-2 tbsp dissolved in cold water then heated until translucent; kuzu-yu with grated ginger and honey is the classic early-cold remedy. Kakkon-to granules per package.
safety: Phytoestrogen - avoid in hormone-sensitive cancers (breast, uterine, ovarian) or consult your oncologist. May add to diabetes medications (hypoglycemia), anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs. Can potentiate methotrexate and tamoxifen; may interact with CYP450-metabolized drugs.
origin: Kakkon-to, the kudzu decoction, is one of Kampo's most prescribed formulas for early colds and stiff shoulders.

name: Umeboshi
aka: pickled Japanese plum, Prunus mume, bainiku ekisu
summary: Ume extracts show antibacterial activity against H. pylori, S. aureus and E. coli, a Wakayama Medical University study linked ume intake to improved gastric motility and less H. pylori gastritis, and mumefural inhibits platelet aggregation.
how: 1-2 umeboshi daily with rice or dissolved in hot water or tea; concentrated ume extract 1/2 tsp daily; umeboshi vinegar 1 tsp in water as a digestive tonic. Paste form is convenient.
safety: Very high sodium (~22% salt traditionally) - limit to 1-2 daily, especially with hypertension or sodium restriction; low-salt versions exist. Intensely sour and may aggravate acid reflux. Anti-platelet effect at high intake - caution with anticoagulants.
origin: The 'king of alkaline foods' in Japanese folk medicine; samurai carried them against fatigue.

name: Miso
summary: In a 90,000-person Japanese cohort, daily miso soup was not linked to higher blood pressure despite its sodium, and fermented soy tracked with lower all-cause mortality; higher intake is also associated with lower breast cancer risk and greater gut microbial diversity (complementary support, not treatment).
how: 1-3 bowls of miso soup daily; use unpasteurized (nama) miso stirred in off the heat. Red miso is longer-fermented and higher in antioxidants; white is milder for dressings.
safety: High sodium (~1g per tablespoon), though fermentation appears to buffer the pressor effect. Avoid with soy allergy - fermentation reduces but does not remove allergens. Phytoestrogens: discuss with your oncologist in hormone-receptor-positive cancer. Aged miso contains tyramine - caution with MAO inhibitors.
origin: A 1,300-year staple; the proverb says 'miso is the doctor's foe' (miso wa isha irazu).

name: Natto
aka: fermented soybeans, nattokinase, vitamin K2 MK-7
summary: An RCT found nattokinase 2,000 FU/day for 8 weeks significantly lowered systolic and diastolic blood pressure, a 29,000-person cohort linked natto specifically to reduced cardiovascular mortality, and MK-7 180mcg/day for 3 years significantly slowed bone loss in postmenopausal women.
how: One pack (40-50g) daily with mustard and soy sauce over rice; or nattokinase 2,000-4,000 FU daily on an empty stomach; or MK-7 vitamin K2 100-200mcg/day.
safety: CRITICAL: contraindicated with warfarin - vitamin K2 directly antagonizes it; do not eat natto or take MK-7 on warfarin. Nattokinase is fibrinolytic - do not combine with anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs without physician guidance, and stop 2 weeks before surgery. Avoid with soy allergy; tyramine content - caution with MAO inhibitors.
origin: A 1,000-year eastern Japanese longevity food; the saying goes 'natto cures a hundred ailments'.

name: Seaweed / Kelp
summary: Fucoxanthin in wakame raised resting energy expenditure and cut abdominal fat in an RCT; kombu is a rich iodine source, and fucoidan shows immunomodulatory activity in lab and animal work only (complementary support, not treatment).
how: Kombu: a 5cm strip cooked with beans or grains, or for dashi. Wakame 5-10g rehydrated daily. Nori 2-3 sheets daily. Fucoidan extracts 100-400mg/day.
safety: Iodine excess is a real risk, mainly from kombu, and can cause both hyper- and hypothyroidism - limit kombu and monitor if you have thyroid disease. Seaweed concentrates arsenic, cadmium and lead; several countries advise against hijiki. May interact with levothyroxine and with anticoagulants (fucoidan is anti-clotting). High potassium - caution in kidney disease.
origin: Eaten in Japan for over 10,000 years; kombu is the base of dashi and the original source of umami.

name: Shiitake, Maitake and Enoki Mushrooms
aka: Lentinula edodes, Grifola frondosa, lentinan, D-fraction
summary: A 4-week RCT found 5-10g dried shiitake daily improved immune markers (SIgA, CRP, T-cell function) in healthy adults; lentinan is an approved injectable adjuvant used alongside conventional gastric cancer care in Japan, and maitake D-fraction enhances NK cell activity as complementary support.
how: Shiitake 5-10g dried (or 100-150g fresh) daily - sun-drying gill-side up for 30 minutes raises vitamin D2 sharply. Maitake 3-7g dried daily or D-fraction extract per label. Enoki 100-150g fresh in soups. Beta-glucan extracts 250-500mg daily.
safety: Very safe as food; allergic reactions rare. Beta-glucans stimulate immunity - consult your physician if on immunosuppressants for transplant or autoimmune disease. Maitake may potentiate hypoglycemic medications. Raw shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis; cook thoroughly.
origin: Shiitake was called the 'elixir of life'; maitake means 'dancing mushroom' for the joy of finding it.

name: Yuzu
summary: A controlled study found 10 minutes of yuzu aromatherapy significantly reduced salivary cortisol, heart rate and psychological tension, comparable to lavender; yuzu peel extract also out-performed lemon and grapefruit peel on antioxidant activity.
how: Yuzu-yu bath: float 2-3 whole or sliced yuzu in hot water and soak 15-20 minutes. Use juice and zest in cooking. Korean yuja-cha: dissolve 1-2 tbsp yuja marmalade in hot water, 1-2 cups daily in cold season. Diffuse the essential oil.
safety: Avoid with citrus allergy. Peel oils cause photosensitivity - keep treated skin out of direct sun. Furanocoumarins may interact with CYP3A4-metabolized drugs (grapefruit-type interaction), though at lower levels than grapefruit. Commercial yuja-cheong is roughly 50% sugar.
origin: The winter-solstice yuzu bath (yuzu-yu) is a centuries-old Japanese ritual to ward off colds.

name: Ginger
summary: A Cochrane Review confirmed ginger is effective for pregnancy-related nausea, with RCT support for chemotherapy-induced, postoperative and motion-sickness nausea; an RCT of 261 patients showed reduced knee osteoarthritis pain, and 250mg four times daily matched ibuprofen for menstrual pain.
how: 1-2g fresh grated ginger daily in tea, food or smoothies; tea from 2-3cm sliced root steeped 10-15 minutes; nausea: 250mg capsules four times daily; dried powder 1/4-1/2 tsp.
safety: May increase bleeding risk - use caution with anticoagulants and stop 1-2 weeks before surgery. May lower blood sugar; monitor if on diabetes medication. Over 6g can cause heartburn and diarrhea. Promotes bile secretion - consult your physician if you have gallstones. Generally safe in pregnancy up to 1g/day.
origin: A cornerstone of Kampo, where fresh shokyo warms the surface for colds and dried kankyo warms the core.

name: Rice Bran
aka: komenuka, nuka, gamma-oryzanol, rice bran oil
summary: A 5-week RCT found rice bran oil lowered LDL cholesterol by 7%, credited to gamma-oryzanol and plant sterols; gamma-oryzanol has been a Japanese pharmaceutical for hyperlipidemia and menopausal symptoms since the 1960s, and rice bran extracts improved skin hydration in clinical trials.
how: Rice bran oil 1-2 tbsp/day as a high-smoke-point cooking oil; gamma-oryzanol supplements 100-300mg/day; nuka-zuke pickles; rice bran in a cloth sachet as a bath-time exfoliant.
safety: Contains phytic acid, which reduces mineral absorption (fermentation partly degrades it). Calorie-dense oil. Rice bran can concentrate arsenic from rice - buy from reputable suppliers. Gamma-oryzanol may interact with thyroid medications and cholesterol drugs.
origin: Japanese households used nuka for centuries as food, pickling bed and a skin-smoothing beauty scrub.

name: Sake Lees
summary: Sake kasu peptides act as ACE inhibitors and lowered blood pressure in animal models, its resistant protein reduced cholesterol absorption in animals, and alpha-ethyl glucoside promoted collagen production in dermal fibroblasts. Human trials are lacking.
how: Amazake: 1 warm cup daily, also usable as a natural sweetener. Sake kasu paste added to soups, marinades and pickles. Face mask: mix to a paste with water, apply 10-15 minutes, rinse.
safety: Contains 5-8% residual alcohol - avoid if alcohol-sensitive or pregnant, and do not give to children unless cooked off. Contains sugar; moderate if diabetic. Koji-based amazake is alcohol-free and preferable for daily use.
origin: The byproduct of sake brewing; brewery workers' famously smooth hands inspired its beauty use.

name: Mugwort / Yomogi
aka: Artemisia princeps, Artemisia vulgaris, ssuk, moxa
summary: A Cochrane Review found moxibustion with mugwort at acupoint BL67 effective for correcting breech presentation; Artemisia princeps extracts inhibit NF-kB and nitric oxide production, and its compounds are antispasmodic, supporting traditional use for menstrual pain.
how: Yomogi tea: 1-2 tsp dried mugwort steeped in hot water, 1-3 times daily. Yomogi mochi as a seasonal food. Add a bundle of dried mugwort to a hot bath. For moxibustion, see a qualified acupuncturist.
safety: Contraindicated in pregnancy - uterine stimulant with miscarriage risk. Mugwort allergy is common, especially with ragweed and chrysanthemum sensitivity, and cross-reacts with celery, carrot and spices. Artemisia compounds can be hepatotoxic at high doses.
origin: The herb burned in moxibustion (okyu) in Kampo, and eaten as yomogi mochi and Korean ssuk soup.

name: Japanese Knotweed
aka: itadori, Fallopia japonica, Polygonum cuspidatum, resveratrol
summary: The world's richest source of trans-resveratrol, which activates SIRT1 and AMPK; a 30-day RCT in obese humans improved inflammation and insulin sensitivity, though cardiovascular trial results are mixed and bioavailability remains a major limitation.
how: Trans-resveratrol supplements (usually knotweed-derived) 150-500mg/day; look for standardization to 50% trans-resveratrol from Polygonum cuspidatum root. Young shoots are edible in spring with a rhubarb-like tartness.
safety: Emodin in the root is a laxative - high doses cause diarrhea and cramping. Resveratrol may add to anticoagulants, antiplatelet drugs and NSAIDs (bleeding risk) and may interact with CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 substrates. Possible estrogenic activity - discuss with your oncologist in hormone-sensitive cancer. High doses cause headache and kidney complaints.
origin: Called itadori, 'pain-remover'; a valued Kampo root and spring vegetable, though invasive in the West.

name: Adzuki Beans
summary: Adzuki extract showed significant alpha-glucosidase inhibition, suggesting acarbose-like blood sugar lowering, and the beans had the highest antioxidant capacity of several varieties tested; saponins support the folk use as a mild diuretic for edema.
how: Cook and eat 1/2 to 1 cup daily in soups, salads or grain bowls. Adzuki bean tea: boil the beans and drink the cooking water as a gentle diuretic. Traditional sekihan pairs them with sticky rice.
safety: Very safe. Contains phytic acid and lectins - boil 30+ minutes to destroy lectins. Diuretic at high intake; stay hydrated. Moderate purine content - caution with gout.
origin: One of the 'five sacred grains' of ancient Japan, used in Kampo as a mild diuretic and detoxifier.

name: Daikon Radish
aka: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus, daikon-oroshi, kaiware
summary: Grating raw daikon activates myrosinase, releasing isothiocyanates that induce Phase II detoxification enzymes via Nrf2 - a mechanism studied as complementary support for cancer risk reduction, not treatment. Its diastase enzyme genuinely aids starch digestion.
how: Freshly grated raw daikon as a condiment with grilled fish, tempura or noodles; juice with apple as a digestive tonic; daikon with honey for sore throat; cooked in oden or as dried kiriboshi strips.
safety: Raw daikon in quantity causes gas and bloating. Goitrogenic compounds may affect thyroid function in iodine-deficient people at very high raw intake. No significant drug interactions at dietary doses.
origin: 'The great root' has been a Japanese staple and digestive folk remedy for over 1,000 years.

name: Soba (Buckwheat)
summary: Buckwheat consumption is associated with lower total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides; its rutin strengthens capillary walls and is used pharmaceutically in Europe for chronic venous insufficiency, while D-chiro-inositol improved insulin sensitivity in women with PCOS.
how: Choose 100% buckwheat (juwari) soba noodles - most commercial soba contains wheat. Sobacha: steep roasted buckwheat groats, caffeine-free, drink freely. Groats in porridge or salads.
safety: Buckwheat allergy is a significant concern in Japan and Korea and can cause severe anaphylaxis. Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free but cross-contamination with wheat is common - verify if celiac. Fagopyrin can cause photosensitivity at very high doses, mainly from green plant parts.
origin: An Edo-period staple; toshi-koshi soba on New Year's Eve symbolizes a long life.

name: Sencha and Hojicha
aka: Japanese steamed green tea, roasted green tea
summary: Sencha, Japan's everyday tea, carries moderate EGCG with more vitamin C than matcha and is associated with the cardiovascular benefits seen in Japanese cohorts; hojicha is roasted, cutting caffeine by about half and adding calming pyrazines.
how: Sencha: brew at 70-80C for 60-90 seconds, 3-5 cups daily. Hojicha: brew at 90-100C for 30-60 seconds; gentle enough for evening, children and sensitive stomachs.
safety: Same caffeine considerations as green tea, though lower - limit if sensitive or pregnant. Tea tannins reduce iron absorption; drink between meals if iron-deficient.
origin: Sencha is the most consumed tea in Japan; hojicha was traditionally given to children and the elderly.

name: Japanese Persimmon
summary: Persimmon tannins bind bile acids, lowering cholesterol, and kakishibu (tannin extract) showed potent antiviral activity against norovirus and influenza; persimmon leaf tea was antihypertensive in animal models, and tannin binds acetaldehyde, supporting the hangover tradition.
how: 1-2 fresh fruits daily in autumn - Fuyu can be eaten crisp, astringent Hachiya must be fully soft. Hoshigaki (dried) 1-2 per day. Persimmon leaf tea 2-3 cups daily. Eat a persimmon before or after drinking alcohol.
safety: Bezoar risk: large amounts of unripe astringent persimmon, especially on an empty stomach or with protein, can form hard stomach masses. May lower blood pressure - caution with antihypertensives. High sugar, especially dried - monitor if diabetic.
origin: The 'fruit of the gods'; the calyx is used in Kampo (shi-di) to stop hiccups.

name: Tsubaki (Camellia Oil)
summary: About 85% oleic acid plus squalene and vitamin E; a clinical evaluation found camellia oil superior to olive oil for moisturizing and skin-barrier repair, and it improved hair tensile strength while reducing cuticle damage.
how: Hair: 3-5 drops on damp hair or dry ends. Face: 2-3 drops as a night moisturizer or mixed into serum. Body: apply after bathing. Also used as a delicate finishing cooking oil on the Izu Islands.
safety: Very safe topically; rare allergic reactions - patch test first. Many commercial products are cut with cheaper oils, so verify purity.
origin: Japan's premier beauty oil for 1,200 years, used by geisha for hair and skin.

name: Onsen / Hot Spring Therapy
summary: A Cochrane Review found moderate evidence that balneotherapy helps chronic low back pain and rheumatoid arthritis, a meta-analysis showed reduced pain and improved function in osteoarthritis, and sulfur-rich bathing significantly improved psoriasis severity in a controlled trial.
how: Soak at 38-42C for 15-20 minutes. At home, add Epsom salt, Dead Sea salts or Japanese onsen mineral powders to the bath.
safety: Avoid with uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure, or in pregnancy (keep below 38C). Hypotension and dizziness on standing are common - rise slowly. Sulfur springs irritate open wounds and sensitive skin. Dehydration risk - drink before and after. Do not submerge your head (rare Naegleria risk). Supervise children closely.
origin: Japan has ~27,000 hot springs and a 1,000-year toji tradition, with a recognized medical specialty in balneology.

name: Korean Red Ginseng
aka: Panax ginseng C.A. Meyer, hongsam, ginsenosides
summary: Systematic reviews of multiple RCTs found Korean red ginseng significantly improved erectile function and enhanced NK and T-cell activity; trials also show better working memory, fewer colds in elderly adults, and 2g/day reduced cancer-related fatigue as complementary support during care.
how: Standardized extract 200-400mg/day (4-7% ginsenosides), or simmer 3-6g root slices 1-2 hours. Traditional cycling: 2-3 months on, 1 month off.
safety: Insomnia and overstimulation are the commonest side effects - take in the morning. May raise blood pressure; monitor if hypertensive. Estrogenic effects may affect hormone-sensitive conditions. Interacts with warfarin (conflicting reports), MAO inhibitors, diabetes drugs (additive hypoglycemia) and immunosuppressants. Avoid under 12, in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Over 3g/day risks 'ginseng abuse syndrome'.
origin: The 'king of herbs' in Hanbang for 2,000 years; steaming converts ginsenosides to more active forms.

name: Fermented Red Ginseng
aka: compound K ginseng, black ginseng extract
summary: Lactobacillus fermentation converts major ginsenosides into compound K, absorbed 5-15 times better; fermented red ginseng showed greater bioavailability and stronger anti-fatigue effects than standard red ginseng, and improved arterial stiffness and blood pressure in hypertensive patients.
how: Follow manufacturer dosing - typically lower than non-fermented product because absorption is greater. Sold as liquid extracts, capsules and sachets.
safety: All Korean red ginseng cautions apply: insomnia and overstimulation, possible blood pressure rise, estrogenic effects, and interactions with warfarin, MAO inhibitors, diabetes medications and immunosuppressants. Enhanced potency means stronger side effects at equivalent doses - start low. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children.
origin: A modern refinement of traditional red ginseng processing using bacterial fermentation.

name: Kimchi and Korean Fermented Foods
summary: The landmark Stanford Cell study (2021) found a 10-week high-fermented-food diet including kimchi significantly increased microbiome diversity and lowered IL-6; a 4-week kimchi trial reduced body weight, BMI and fasting glucose in overweight adults.
how: 1-2 servings (~100g) of unpasteurized live-culture kimchi daily. Doenjang in soups and marinades; cheonggukjang in stew for its fibrinolytic enzyme and vitamin K2.
safety: High sodium (~750mg per 100g) - limit with hypertension or sodium restriction. Some Korean studies link very high kimchi intake to increased gastric cancer risk (sodium and N-nitroso compounds), likely dose-dependent and offset by probiotic benefits. High histamine - caution with histamine intolerance; tyramine - caution with MAO inhibitors. Introduce gradually to avoid gas and bloating.
origin: A 2,000-year-old cornerstone of Korean cuisine; kimjang is UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.

name: Gochujang
summary: A 12-week study found gochujang consumption in overweight women was associated with reduced visceral fat and improved metabolic markers; capsaicin activates TRPV1 to modestly raise metabolic rate and reduce appetite, and fermentation boosts antioxidant activity.
how: Use as a condiment, 1-2 tsp per serving; mix with sesame oil and vinegar for bibimbap sauce; add to marinades, stews and dipping sauces. Aged (3+ year) gochujang has richer bioactive content.
safety: Capsaicin can aggravate GERD, gastritis, IBS and hemorrhoids. Very high sodium content. Avoid with nightshade sensitivity. May interact with anticoagulants since capsaicin affects platelet function.
origin: A 500-year-old Korean staple, sun-aged in onggi earthenware jars for months to years.

name: Korean Angelica
summary: Decursin, unique to this species, showed anti-cancer activity against prostate cancer cells and inhibited angiogenesis in animal models - preclinical complementary-support research only, not a treatment. Extracts were also neuroprotective against amyloid-beta toxicity and anti-inflammatory via NF-kB inhibition.
how: Dried root decoction: simmer 6-12g in water 30-60 minutes, 1-2 cups daily. Usually taken within Hanbang multi-herb formulas; supplements are standardized to decursin.
safety: Coumarin derivatives may interact with anticoagulants. Furanocoumarins cause phytophotodermatitis - sun sensitivity. Avoid in pregnancy (potential uterine stimulant). Do not confuse with toxic Apiaceae relatives such as water hemlock; buy from reputable suppliers for correct species.
origin: A key Hanbang 'blood deficiency' herb for women's health and a component of Ssanghwa-tang.

name: Ssanghwa-tang
summary: This nine-herb tonic (rehmannia, cnidium, white peony, Korean angelica, astragalus, cinnamon, licorice, jujube, ginger) showed immunomodulatory effects on macrophages and anti-fatigue effects in swim-endurance animal models; human trial evidence is limited.
how: Pre-made ssanghwa-tang pouches (100-120mL) once daily during fatigue or recovery, sold in Korean groceries and convenience stores. Traditional custom decoctions come from a Hanbang practitioner; often taken with a raw egg yolk stirred in.
safety: Contains cassia cinnamon, whose coumarin can stress the liver at high doses. Contains licorice, which raises blood pressure and depletes potassium with prolonged use. Rehmannia may interact with diabetes medications. Consult a practitioner if you have chronic conditions.
origin: One of Korea's most famous recovery tonics, prescribed after illness, postpartum and for chronic fatigue.

name: Omija (Schisandra)
summary: Classified as an adaptogen by the EMA, schisandra modulates the HPA axis and cortisol in stress models; schisandrin B protects the liver against CCl4, acetaminophen and alcohol injury by boosting glutathione, and its derivative DDB is an approved hepatoprotective drug in several Asian countries.
how: Omija-cha: steep dried berries in cold water overnight or infuse hot; sweeten with honey, 1-2 cups daily. Standardized extract 500-1000mg/day; tincture 2-4mL two to three times daily. Often paired with rhodiola and eleuthero.
safety: May cause heartburn, appetite loss or stomach upset, and increases stomach acid - caution with ulcers or GERD. Affects CYP3A4 metabolism and can therefore interact with many pharmaceuticals. Avoid in pregnancy (uterine stimulant potential). Caution with anti-epileptic drugs.
origin: Named for holding all five tastes; a prized Korean adaptogen and classic summer tea.

name: Korean Mistletoe
summary: Korean mistletoe lectins showed anti-tumor and NK-cell-stimulating effects in animal and in vitro work, and a pilot trial found extract improved quality of life in hepatocellular carcinoma patients receiving chemotherapy - complementary support alongside oncology care, never a treatment. European mistletoe has far more human data.
how: Used only as a professionally prepared extract under practitioner guidance, typically via Korean traditional medicine clinics. This is not a DIY herb.
safety: All parts of the raw plant are toxic and the berries are poisonous - never consume wild mistletoe. Must be professionally prepared and administered. May interact with immunosuppressants, antihypertensives and anticoagulants. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: A Korean folk remedy for joint pain and hypertension, distinct from European Iscador preparations.

name: Perilla Oil
summary: The richest plant source of alpha-linolenic acid (54-64%, exceeding flaxseed); a clinical trial found perilla oil significantly reduced TNF-alpha and IL-6, and another showed improved lipid profiles (lower triglycerides, higher HDL) in hyperlipidemic subjects.
how: Use as a finishing oil only - the smoke point is about 160C and omega-3s degrade with heat. 1-2 tsp daily drizzled on vegetables, noodles, rice or salads; capsules available as an omega-3 supplement.
safety: Oxidizes quickly - store in dark glass in the refrigerator and use within 2-3 months of opening. May add to anticoagulant effects through its omega-3 antiplatelet action. Calorie-dense (~120 kcal/tbsp). Buy food-grade only.
origin: A defining flavor of Korean cooking, traditionally valued as cooling and used for cough and asthma.

name: Korean Licorice
summary: In a 1985 Gut RCT, deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) healed gastric ulcers as effectively as cimetidine; glycyrrhizin shows in vitro antiviral activity against SARS-CoV, hepatitis C and influenza.
how: DGL chewable tablets 380-760mg before meals - the safest long-term form. Licorice tea: 1-2g dried root, 1-3 times daily, short-term only (2-4 weeks).
safety: Glycyrrhizin causes pseudoaldosteronism - prolonged or high-dose use causes sodium retention, potassium depletion, hypertension and edema, which can be dangerous. Contraindicated in hypertension, heart failure, kidney disease, hypokalemia and cirrhosis. Interacts with potassium-depleting diuretics, digoxin, corticosteroids and warfarin. Avoid in pregnancy (premature birth risk). Cap whole licorice at ~100mg glycyrrhizin (3g root)/day for 4-6 weeks.
origin: The 'great harmonizer' of Hanbang, included in most Korean herbal formulas to balance other herbs.

name: Jujube
summary: Jujube seed extract is among the best-supported herbal sedatives: jujuboside A modulates GABAergic neurotransmission, and a 2020 systematic review found it significantly improved sleep quality across multiple clinical trials. Its polysaccharides also enhance macrophage and NK cell activity.
how: Eat 3-5 dried jujubes daily, or simmer 10-15 in water 30 minutes for daechu-cha before bed. For sleep specifically, jujube seed extract 250-500mg standardized at bedtime. Also used in samgyetang with ginseng and garlic.
safety: Dried jujubes are ~70% sugar - moderate if diabetic or managing weight. May potentiate sedative medications including benzodiazepines and barbiturates. Otherwise one of the gentlest herbs in the Korean pharmacopoeia; large amounts can cause bloating.
origin: A 3,000-year staple used to 'tonify the spleen and stomach, nourish blood and calm the spirit'.

name: Pine Nut Oil
summary: In a double-blind crossover RCT, Korean pine nut oil raised the satiety hormones CCK-8 and GLP-1 about 60% more than olive oil in overweight women, reducing appetite; pinolenic acid also lowers LDL by enhancing hepatic LDL receptor activity.
how: 1-2 tsp of pine nut oil 30-60 minutes before meals for appetite management. Eat pine nuts in salads, pesto and porridge; jat-juk (pine nut porridge) is a traditional convalescent breakfast.
safety: 'Pine mouth' - a lingering bitter or metallic taste for days to weeks - occurs with some pine nut species, more often Chinese than Korean. Pine nuts are seeds but may cross-react with tree nut allergies. Calorie-dense; expensive and sometimes adulterated.
origin: A luxury Korean ingredient traditionally used for dry skin, hair care and as a digestive aid.

name: Korean Bellflower Root
summary: Platycodin D stimulates airway mucus secretion and promotes expectoration - well documented and the basis for its inclusion in Korean OTC cough medicines - and it inhibits NF-kB, reducing TNF-alpha, IL-1B and IL-6 in macrophages.
how: Doraji-cha: simmer 5-10g dried root 20-30 minutes and drink for sore throat and cough. Doraji-cheong (root preserved in honey) dissolved in hot water. Doraji-namul as a seasoned side dish; also in standardized extracts and cough syrups.
safety: Saponins can cause nausea, vomiting or diarrhea at high doses, with hemolytic activity at very high concentrations (not a concern at dietary levels). Limited pregnancy safety data - avoid or consult a practitioner. Safe as food at culinary doses.
origin: One of Korea's most important 'lung herbs', used to open the lungs and expel phlegm.

name: Acorn Jelly
summary: Acorn jelly consumption was associated with a reduced postprandial blood glucose response compared with rice, and its tannins are astringent (traditionally used for diarrhea) and can chelate heavy metals in the gut; it is very low calorie at ~35 kcal per 100g.
how: Slice dotori-muk and serve with seasoned soy sauce as a side dish or snack; dotori-guksu acorn noodles as a low-glycemic noodle alternative. Acorn starch powder is sold in Korean groceries for home preparation.
safety: Raw acorns contain toxic levels of tannins - proper leaching is essential and raw acorns must never be eaten. Excess tannin impairs iron absorption and can cause constipation. Safe when properly prepared.
origin: A Korean famine food for centuries, believed to 'clean out' the body after heavy meals.

name: Barley Tea
summary: Roasting creates melanoidins with antioxidant, prebiotic and antimicrobial properties; roasted barley tea showed antioxidant activity and inhibited bacterial adhesion to teeth, and it is a caffeine-free, virtually calorie-free replacement for sugary drinks.
how: Boil 2-3 tbsp roasted barley (or 1-2 tea bags) in 1-2 litres of water for 10-15 minutes, then cool and refrigerate. Drink freely hot or cold, suitable for all ages.
safety: Contains gluten - not suitable for celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. Otherwise among the safest items in this guide; observe normal hygiene when steeping grains.
origin: Korea's default daily beverage, served free at restaurants and drunk to cool the body in summer.

name: Corn Silk Tea
summary: Corn silk extract showed significant diuretic activity in animal models, increasing urine volume while sparing potassium (unlike pharmaceutical diuretics), plus hypoglycemic and anti-inflammatory effects; one clinical study linked it to reduced kidney stone formation.
how: Steep 2-3g dried corn silk in boiling water 10-15 minutes, 2-3 cups daily. Pre-packaged tea bags are sold in Korean groceries, or collect and dry fresh silk in season.
safety: Diuretic - stay hydrated and note it may enhance prescribed diuretics. May lower blood sugar (monitor with diabetes medication) and blood pressure (caution with antihypertensives). Avoid with corn allergy. Potential warfarin interaction via vitamin K. Insufficient data in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: A popular Korean folk remedy using the silk of corn as a gentle kidney and urinary tonic.

name: Solomon's Seal Tea
summary: Polygonatum polysaccharides improved insulin sensitivity in diabetic animal models and showed immunomodulatory and antioxidant effects; its mucilage gives a demulcent, soothing action on dry throat and GI membranes, matching traditional use for dry cough and thirst.
how: Steep 5-10g roasted Solomon's seal root in hot water 5-10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily; the flavor is sweet and mild. Sold as roasted root slices or tea bags; often combined with jujube.
safety: Very safe at tea doses. May lower blood sugar - monitor if diabetic. Some Polygonatum species contain cardiac glycosides at very high doses, so stay within tea quantities. Never confuse with False Solomon's Seal or the toxic Lily of the Valley.
origin: A classic Hanbang 'yin-nourishing' tea for dry cough, dry throat and fatigue.

name: Shinrin-Yoku (Forest Bathing)
summary: Dr. Qing Li showed a 3-day forest trip raised NK cell activity 50% for over 30 days (urban walks did not), and vaporized hinoki phytoncides alone raised it 20%; across 24 forests, forest settings cut salivary cortisol 12.4% and lowered blood pressure.
how: Walk slowly through mature woodland with no destination - 2 hours is ideal, 15-20 minutes measurably helps. Engage all senses, phone silent, sit still, breathe deeply, weekly. Diffusing hinoki or pine oil helps indoors.
safety: Watch for ticks, snakes and poisonous plants; pollen seasons may limit benefit. Not a replacement for mental health treatment in severe conditions - use as an adjunct. Tell someone your location.
origin: Coined by Japan's Forestry Ministry in 1982, drawing on Shinto and Buddhist reverence for forests.

name: Jjimjilbang / Sauna Therapy
summary: In 2,315 Finnish men followed 20 years, sauna use 4-7 times weekly was associated with 63% lower sudden cardiac death and 40% lower all-cause mortality; Waon therapy trials improved cardiac function in chronic heart failure.
how: 15-20 minutes per session at 80-100C dry or 60C infrared, 2-7 times weekly, alternating hot and cool rooms with rest and water between.
safety: Contraindicated in unstable angina, recent heart attack, severe aortic stenosis and uncontrolled hypertension. Drink 500mL water per 15-minute session; add electrolytes with heavy use. NEVER combine with alcohol (hypotension, arrhythmia). Frequent use temporarily lowers sperm count. In pregnancy keep core temperature under 38.9C. Elderly: fall and hypotension risk. Can worsen rosacea.
origin: Korean heated bathhouses with charcoal, jade, salt and clay rooms, tied to the ondol heated-floor tradition.

name: Japanese Water Therapy
summary: The disease-curing claims are overstated, but some elements hold: water on an empty stomach triggers the gastrocolic reflex and eases constipation, 500mL raises metabolic rate ~30% briefly, and pre-meal water cut intake ~75 kcal with weight loss over 12 weeks.
how: On waking, sip 500mL-1L of room-temperature or warm water over 5-10 minutes, then wait 30-45 minutes before breakfast. Stay at 2-3L total daily.
safety: Hyponatremia risk - drinking over 1.5L quickly without electrolytes can dangerously dilute blood sodium; never force intake. Kidney disease impairs water clearance - consult your physician. Heart failure may require fluid restriction. Increase gradually to avoid nausea. Not a substitute for medical treatment.
origin: A Japanese folk practice, echoed in Ayurveda, of drinking water immediately upon waking.

name: Shiatsu and Acupressure
aka: PC6 Neiguan, LI4 Hegu, SP6, HT7, ST36, GV20, LV3, Sea-Band
summary: A Cochrane Review of 59 trials (~7,600 people) found PC6 wrist acupressure significantly reduced postoperative nausea, with support for chemotherapy, pregnancy and motion-sickness nausea; LI4 eased headache and labor pain, SP6 dysmenorrhea, HT7 insomnia.
how: Press firmly with thumb or fingertip 1-3 minutes per point, breathing slowly, 2-3 times daily. PC6 sits three finger-widths above the wrist crease between the tendons - Sea-Band wristbands hold pressure there.
safety: SP6 is contraindicated in pregnancy except under practitioner guidance at full term (uterine stimulation). Never press open wounds, fractures, varicose veins or inflamed skin. Avoid deep pressure over tumor sites (gentle work only with oncologist approval) and on legs with DVT history. Not a substitute for emergency care.
origin: A Japanese finger-pressure therapy from anma massage and Chinese acupressure, recognized by Japan's Health Ministry.
